Past Fairs: Paris Photo 2023
The presentation of alignDRAW by @elmanmansimov

Three years ago, we took a chance on presenting the alignDRAW collection at Paris Photo 2023. alignDRAW is one of the first text-to-image generation models, created by Elman Mansimov in 2015 as an undergraduate at the University of Toronto. The images are low resolution, just 32 by 32 pixels, made years before the field's more recent advances.

In the essay that follows, @dariushimes, International Head of Photographs at Christie's, situates Mansimov's work within a much longer lineage, tracing the human urge to make images from the earliest cave paintings through the invention of photography and into this new computational chapter.

Advance Frontier: The Work of @elmanmansimov ↓

The human impulse, is it a need, or a propensity, or possibly a calling?, to make marks and create images stretches back to the beginning of human consciousness, as far as we can tell. Every region of the globe exhibits ancient glyphs of some kind, the Nazca lines of Peru, the Tassili n'Ajjer in Algeria, the Bhimbetka rock shelters in India, and of course the famous caves of Lascaux and Chauvet in France, and Altamira on the Iberian Peninsula. Rudimentary figures of bison, horses, deer, and other humans were etched and painted with astonishing skill tens of thousands of years ago. The precise meaning of these marks has remained shrouded in mystery, and has been debated for generations. Perhaps documentary in nature, the imagery recorded hunts and moments of valor; it may have been a symbolic form of conjuring or pre-visualization, or simply the earliest form of self-portraiture. Whatever its purpose, it testifies to a compulsion to preserve presence, to extend perception, to take what is seen or felt and fix it against the erasure of time.

Centuries later, this impulse for image making was codified in innumerable varieties as pictographs and hieroglyphs. Various languages and ancient scripts emerged that were based on the image, not just a representative symbol of sound. Both the hieroglyphs of ancient Egypt and the oracle bone script of ancient China are examples. These images were not decoration alone but a functioning system, a language where stylized depictions of mountains, birds, and serpents stood for sounds, ideas, and deities. The pictorial instinct here was institutionalized, placed in the service of religion, governance, and memory. Tomb paintings carried this dual purpose further, fusing the visual with the symbolic. Just as the hand stencil declared “I was here,” so the hieroglyphs and murals declared, with greater confidence, “We envision. We remember. We endure.”

The development of Greek sculpture, Roman portraiture, and medieval iconography shows how images came to embody authority. They recorded rulers, instructed the faithful, and enshrined history. The Renaissance, with its rediscovery of perspective, introduced new methods to capture the world with verisimilitude, pushing one step further away from the symbolic and toward the “real.” Artists studied optics and anatomy to bridge the gap between perception and representation. Their goal was not simply beauty, but accuracy, an image that could rival the experience of sight itself.

This relentless pursuit of realism inevitably led us to the discovery of the principles of photography, that marriage of the sciences of optics and chemistry. The child of this marriage was a mirror reflection of the world that only became clearer and clearer over the decades. The camera obscura, long used by painters to trace outlines, was a precursor. In 1826 or 1827, Joseph Nicéphore Niépce made what is now regarded as the first permanent photograph: a grainy view from an upper-story window. Louis Daguerre, working in collaboration with Niépce, soon improved the process, and in 1839 the daguerreotype astonished the world.

Portrait studios spread rapidly; for the first time, ordinary families could obtain faithful likenesses. Memory became externalized and permanent. The photograph was hailed as a miracle and feared as a menace, the death knell of a kind of realistic painting style toward which Western Europeans had gravitated. Artists worried that their vocation might vanish. Philosophers questioned whether this machine-made image could truly be art. The public embraced it with an unrestrained voraciousness. At a time when streets were still cobblestone or dirt and the only source of light after sunset was fire, the miracle of a perfect likeness of a loved one captured on a tiny, mirrored sheet of metal was like a portal to another universe.

The arrival of photography raised questions about objectivity, authorship, and value. Could a machine be creative? Was photography merely mechanical reproduction or could it, for instance in the hands of Julia Margaret Cameron or Alfred Stieglitz, become an expressive medium? These debates reverberated throughout the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Today, these exact same arguments are echoed almost verbatim in discussions about artificial intelligence and art. And it is here, in the third decade of the twenty-first century, that Elman Mansimov enters the story. Born in 1996 in Azerbaijan, Mansimov displayed an early aptitude in mathematics and science. At just fifteen years old, he was admitted to the University of Toronto, where he studied computer science under Ruslan Salakhutdinov, a prominent figure in deep learning. These were the years of AlexNet and the sudden leap forward in neural networks. While others focused on recognition, teaching machines to classify images, Mansimov began to wonder whether they might be taught to create them.

In 2015, while still an undergraduate, Mansimov led a project that produced alignDRAW, the first text-to-image generation model. The results were elementary, low resolution, distorted, filled with strange accidents. But they were recognizably images derived from words: a “yellow school bus,” “a group of elephants.” In that crude material lay the first signs of a profound shift. The machine was no longer a passive observer of images; it had become a participant in making them. Mansimov continued his research at New York University, pursuing a doctorate under Kyunghyun Cho. His work explored iterative refinement in machine learning, methods that allowed systems to improve outputs step by step. Though the technical details belonged to the field of computer science, the implications were far wider.

What began as research into algorithms was, at its core, a new chapter in the history of image making. Mansimov’s career later took him to Amazon Web Services, where he now contributes to large-scale models. Yet outside the laboratory, his early experiments gained unexpected recognition as artifacts of a creative process.

In 2023, his alignDRAW images were exhibited at the annual Paris Photo art fair, a modern acknowledgment of computer science research as cultural artifact. This acknowledgement falls neatly in line with many other examples from the technological development of photography. Cyanotypes of pressed seaweed by Anna Atkins in the 1840s; animal motion studies by Eadweard Muybridge; Édouard Belin’s telegraph-transmitted Bélinographes; and NASA’s images from the surface of the moon, all are examples of scientific research that utilized photography and found its way into the market as highly collectible photographic objects, true artifacts of the scientific process with their own inherent elegance and logic.

The Worcester Art Museum in Massachusetts acquired several of Mansimov’s works, cementing both Mansimov’s and its own institutional place in the canon of image history. By 2024, Mansimov was being included in exhibitions devoted to the pioneers of AI art, recognized not only as a researcher but as a figure whose work bridged science and aesthetics. Asked whether he considered himself an artist, Mansimov has been clear. He views his work as science that, by accident, became art. “It’s very interesting from my perspective because I’m not an artist, right? I’m a computer scientist, and that’s my background, and that’s what I do.”

Niépce likewise did not call himself an artist; he was an inventor. But Louis-Jacques-Mandé Daguerre, William Henry Fox Talbot, and Samuel Morse were likewise all highly educated inventors and deeply cultured, aware of the ramifications of science on art and image making. The results of their inventiveness not only have entered public consciousness, but have been retained and collected by museums and altered the trajectory of art. Mansimov belongs to this same lineage. His alignDRAW images lack photorealistic polish, but they carry the aura of Niépce’s first photograph: hesitant, imperfect, epochal.

The questions surrounding authorship remain pressing. In AI art, is “the artist” Mansimov, who wrote the code; the dataset of millions of images that shaped the model; the user who supplies the prompt; or the system that generates the output? Perhaps all share in authorship, or perhaps the notion of traditional authorship itself is an inadequate framework. What matters is that the impulse to make images has found a new vehicle, one that distributes agency across a network of human and machine actors.

Mansimov himself has argued that new terms may be needed. To directly call these works “photographs” is misleading. They are not captured from light but generated from computation. They are not imprints of reality but inventions constructed from probabilities. They belong to neither painting nor photography, but something that is still emerging. Mansimov’s position is that AI is not a replacement for human creativity but an extension of it, software that expands what is possible, just as the camera once did for painters. “Artists often begin by getting inspired by each other and gradually adding their own voice to their work.” The reception of Mansimov’s work bears out this claim. Audiences have noted that the images, though primitive, hold fascination.

They mark the starting point of a field that, in less than a decade, has advanced from blurred impressions to highly detailed, uncanny visions. And like the earliest photographs, historical importance outweighs matters of immediate beauty. When one surveys the arc from caves to cameras to code, the continuity is clear: Every advance in image making has provoked anxiety. Cave art was once the province of chiefs and shamans; hieroglyphs were guarded by the ecclesiastical class; photography unsettled painters; and AI art now raises its own alarms about authenticity, originality, and value. Yet history suggests that rather than replacing older forms, each new technology expands the field. Photography freed painting to pursue abstraction. AI may, in turn, liberate artists to explore new terrain.

Mansimov’s contribution lies not only in technical ingenuity but in the way it embodies this continuity. He did not seek to be an artist, yet his work is now permanently preserved in museums. He did not set out with aesthetic goals, yet the work carries an artistic ambience. We all stand at a threshold. His alignDRAW work is as much a historical document as Niépce’s heliograph. The fascination with images is not incidental to humanity; it is deep in the veins and consciousness of the human race. From the palm pressed against stone to the algorithm generating pixels, the purpose is the same: to externalize thought, to preserve what passes, to make visible both outer and inner states of awareness. Elman Mansimov, through his early work in AI, has joined that oldest of traditions. His images, however tentative, belong to the lineage of all who have ever tried to capture the world and fix it in an image.

Gen AI vs AI Agents vs Agentic AI.

Most builders confuse these.
Here is the difference.

GEN AI :-
What it does: Generates content
Examples: ChatGPT writing text, Midjourney creating images, GitHub Copilot suggesting code
Input: Prompt
Output: Text, image, code
Limitation: One request, one response. No memory. No action.

AI AGENTS :- 
What it does: Perceives, decides, acts
Examples: Auto-GPT researching a topic, a bot that books flights, a coding assistant that debugs and fixes
Input: Goal
Output: Action + Result
Capabilities: Tool use, memory, iteration, self-correction
Limitation: Single agent. Limited scope.

AGENTIC AI :- 
What it does: Orchestrates multiple agents to solve complex problems
Examples: Research team (researcher + writer + fact-checker), software dev team (architect + coder + reviewer), business automation (sales + support + fulfillment)
Input: Complex objective
Output: Coordinated workflow with multiple agents collaborating
Capabilities: Multi-agent orchestration, consensus, delegation, conflict resolution
Limitation: Complexity, coordination overhead, cost

THE EVOLUTION
Gen AI: "Write me a blog post"
AI Agent: "Research this topic and write a blog post with sources"
Agentic AI: "Run my entire content operation: research, write, edit, fact-check, publish & promote"

WHAT TO BUILD IN 2026

If you are learning Gen AI:
Build structured outputs, RAG systems, prompt chains.

If you are learning AI Agents:
Build tool-using agents with memory, iteration limits, and error handling.

If you are learning Agentic AI:
Build multi-agent swarms with supervisor patterns, consensus logic & human approval gates.

THE TRUTH :-
Gen AI is a tool.
AI Agents are workers.
Agentic AI is an organization.

Most builders stop at Gen AI.

The top 1% are building Agentic systems.
